assessment:
This study by Dong et al. investigates the molecular mechanisms controlling directional migration of Drosophila tracheal progenitor cells during metamorphosis. The authors address an important question in stem cell biology: how do adult stem cells establish and maintain disciplined, directional migration as they exit their niches to regenerate damaged tissue? Using the Drosophila tracheal system as a model, they demonstrate that tracheal progenitors normally migrate in a stereotypical anterior-to-posterior direction along the dorsal trunk, and they identify a novel inter-organ signaling mechanism that controls this process.

The key findings are well-supported by multiple complementary approaches. The authors show that the fat body, an organ anatomically adjacent to the trachea, is essential for maintaining directional progenitor migration. Through RNA-seq analysis, genetic screens, and functional studies, they identify the fat body-derived cytokine Upd2 as the critical signal that activates JAK/STAT signaling in tracheal progenitors. Perturbation of either Upd2 production in fat body or JAK/STAT pathway components in trachea causes aberrant bidirectional migration, demonstrating the necessity of this signaling axis. The mechanistic insights are particularly strong: ChIP-seq analysis reveals that JAK/STAT signaling directly regulates planar cell polarity (PCP) genes, and imaging studies show asymmetric localization of PCP components like Fat at the leading edge of migrating progenitors. The authors further demonstrate that Upd2 is transported from fat body to trachea via vesicles requiring Rab5/Rab7-mediated endocytic sorting and the tetraspanin Lbm, supported by colocalization studies, proximity ligation assays, co-immunoprecipitation, and functional reporter assays.

The experimental design is rigorous with appropriate controls throughout. The use of tissue-specific drivers, temporal control with Gal80ts, multiple independent RNAi lines, genetic mutants, and pharmacological inhibitors provides strong validation of the key findings. Quantitative analyses including migration tracking, entropy measurements, and optic flow analysis add rigor to the characterization of migration phenotypes. The surface proteomics approach to identify trachea-associated proteins is innovative, and the development of the DIPF reporter to monitor ligand-receptor interactions in vivo is technically sophisticated. However, some aspects could be strengthened: the ChIP-seq was performed on whole larval trachea rather than specifically on progenitor cells, which may include non-relevant binding events; the mechanism by which PCP asymmetry translates into directional migration could be more directly tested; and while the vesicular transport of Upd2 is well-documented, the specificity of this mechanism (whether other signals use similar routes) is not fully explored.

This work makes important contributions to understanding stem cell migration and inter-organ communication. The identification of a fat body-to-trachea signaling axis controlling directional migration reveals how metabolic organs can remotely regulate stem cell behavior. The finding that JAK/STAT signaling controls migration directionality (rather than serving as a guidance cue) through regulation of PCP genes provides new mechanistic insights. The demonstration that cytokine transport occurs via tetraspanin-containing vesicles adds to our understanding of how signaling molecules are delivered between organs. The findings have implications beyond Drosophila, as the JAK/STAT pathway, PCP components, and vesicular transport mechanisms are conserved in mammals. The work will be of broad interest to researchers studying stem cell migration, tissue regeneration, inter-organ communication, and planar cell polarity.
